lessons.title: হওয়া (hôwā) — "to be," and the be-verb it stands beside
lessons.gloss: to be, to become — the second of Bengali's two be-verbs, and the one that does what আছে cannot

segments.text: Chapter 2 said "my name Arun" with no verb at all. Chapter 3 put one back for "how are you." Both were right, and this verb is why.
হওয়া — hôwā — to be, to become.
আমি হই (āmi hôi), "I am, I become." সে হয় (se hôy), "he is." Its future is already in your mouth: হবে (hôbe) is the "will happen" inside Chapter 4's dækhā hôbe.

হওয়া (hôwā) is Sanskrit √ভূ (√bhū, "to become") with the bh- worn down to a plain h-: bhavati becomes Prakrit hoï becomes Bengali hô-. The root is PIE bʰuH-, "to grow, to become," and English owns two of its children outright — be and been. Latin built fuī ("I was") and futūrus on it, which is English future; Greek built phúsis, "growth, nature," which is physics.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: হ, and the ওয়া that ends a Bengali verb

segments.text: হ is a soft, breathed h carrying Bengali's inherent vowel — hô, not ha. ওয়া (-wā) is the tail every dictionary-form verb wears; you will meet it again on খাওয়া (khāwā) and যাওয়া (jāwā).

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two be-verbs, and one of them is unfinished

utterances: what you mean: my name is Arun. what Bengali uses: no verb at all.
what you mean: I have a book; it is here. what Bengali uses: আছে (āchhe).
what you mean: he will be a teacher. what Bengali uses: হবে (hôbe).

segments.text: আছ-, the verb behind Chapter 3's kemon āchho, means being present. But it is unfinished: it has a present and a past, and nothing else at all. Push it into the future and it stops dead — so Bengali picks up হ- (hôbe), or Chapter 5's থাকা (āmi thākbo, "I'll be there"). One job, two verbs, split down the middle.

segments.instruction: the future you already knew — "hôbe … dækhā hôbe"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the future you already knew — "hôbe … dækhā hôbe"]

segments.instruction: which verb for "I have a book," and which for "he will be a teacher"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: which verb for "I have a book," and which for "he will be a teacher"]

segments.text: Which Sanskrit root is hôwā, and which two English words are its brothers? (√bhū, "to become" — be and been.) What can আছ- not do? (Anything past a present and a past — it has no future of its own.) So what does Bengali reach for instead? (হবে, or থাকা.) Next: one verb, three levels of respect.

lessons.title: যাওয়া (jāwā) — "to go," and the respect that rides on the ending
lessons.gloss: to go — and the verb ending that carries how much respect you are paying

segments.text: Chapter 2 gave you three different words for "you." It did not tell you the rest of the bill: each one bends the verb a different way too.
যাওয়া — jāwā — to go.
আমি যাই (āmi jāi), "I go." Same -i "I" ending as Chapter 5's bôli, on the same -wā dictionary form you met a moment ago.

যাওয়া (jāwā) is Sanskrit √যা (√yā, "to go, to travel"), and the whole northern family walks on it: Hindi jānā, Marathi jāṇe, Gujarati javũ, Punjabi jāṇā. Sanskrit's y- hardened to a j- sound right across eastern Indo-Aryan, which is why Bengali still writes the y-letter য but says j.

Deeper than Sanskrit it goes to PIE yeh₂-, "to travel" — and here is an honest limit: English kept no everyday word from that root. The nearest living cousin is Lithuanian jóti, "to ride." A fake English cousin here would be worse than none.
য is the letter Sanskrit reads as y; Bengali reads it as j, like জ. So a written yā- is a spoken jā- — an un-shift worth keeping, since it disguises dozens of familiar Sanskrit words.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the respect is not in the pronoun, it is in the ending

utterances: who you are speaking to: তুই (tui, intimate). "you go": যাস (jāsh).
who you are speaking to: তুমি (tumi, familiar). "you go": যাও (jāo).
who you are speaking to: আপনি (āpni, respectful). "you go": যান (jān).

segments.text: Three endings, one verb. And the same grading runs on into the third person: সে যায় (se jāy) is "he goes," তিনি যান (tini jān) is "he goes" said of someone you respect — the very ending আপনি takes. Chapter 5 showed that the ending already means "I," so the pronoun can be dropped. The register cannot. Choose jāsh or jān and you have placed yourself socially, pronoun or no pronoun.

segments.instruction: the two third persons — "se jāy … tini jān"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two third persons — "se jāy … tini jān"]

segments.text: Give the three "you go" forms and who each is for. (Jāsh intimate, jāo familiar, jān respectful.) If you drop the pronoun, is the respect dropped too? (No — it is in the ending, and cannot be dodged.) Does English have a living cousin of this root? (No — Lithuanian jóti is as close as it gets.) Next: the verb that asks nothing about who you are.

lessons.title: আসা (āsā) — "to come," the verb that never asks who you are
lessons.gloss: to come — the verb that never asks whether a man or a woman is speaking

segments.text: Chapter 1's goodbye, āshi, was one form of this verb. Here is the whole of it — and the one question it refuses to ask you.
আসা — āsā — to come.
আমি আসি (āmi āsi), "I come" — the farewell you already own. সে আসে (se āse), "he comes." আপনি আসেন (āpni āsen), with last lesson's respectful ending.

The আ- in front is Sanskrit's ā-, "hither, toward" — the very prefix that turns going into coming. Hindi's ānā is that ā- welded onto yā-, the go-verb of the last lesson: "go, but this way." Bengali shows the same prefix on a different stem, and the honest position on that stem is that its history is unsettled; this book will not invent one for it.

স is written for s and spoken, in this word, as sh — Bengali's standing s becomes sh tilt, the same one that makes namaskāra into nômoshkar. So আসি is āshi, not āsi, though the dictionary form is romanized āsā.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: no gender, not here, not anywhere

utterances: language: Hindi. "I come," man / woman: maiṁ ātā hūṁ / maiṁ ātī hūṁ.
language: Marathi. "I come," man / woman: mī yeto / mī yete.
language: Bengali. "I come," man / woman: āmi āsi — one form.

segments.text: Its sisters make you declare your gender to say the plainest thing in the world. Bengali does not. And this is not a shortcut for beginners that the grammar takes back later: Bengali has no grammatical gender at all. Not on verbs, not on nouns, not on adjectives. The past behaves the same way — আমি এলাম (āmi elām), "I came," is one form for everyone, where Gujarati, which hides gender in its present, brings it straight back in huṁ āvyo / huṁ āvī.

segments.instruction: the neighbours splitting in two — "ātā … ātī" and "yeto … yete"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the neighbours splitting in two — "ātā … ātī" and "yeto … yete"]

segments.instruction: Bengali not splitting — "āmi āsi" — and its past, "āmi elām"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: Bengali not splitting — "āmi āsi" — and its past, "āmi elām"]

segments.text: What does the আ- on this verb mean, and where else have you met it? (Hither, toward — it is the ā- inside Hindi's ānā.) How many forms of "I come" does a Bengali speaker need? (One — āmi āsi, whoever is talking.) Is that true of the nouns too? (Yes — Bengali has no grammatical gender anywhere.) Next: a verb that swallows more than food.

lessons.title: খাওয়া (khāwā) — "to eat," and the drinking it also does
lessons.gloss: to eat — and, in everyday Bengali, to drink as well

segments.text: Every verb so far has meant roughly what its English gloss means. This one is wider than its gloss, and the extra width is the lesson.
খাওয়া — khāwā — to eat.
আমি খাই (āmi khāi), "I eat." আপনি খান (āpni khān), with the respectful ending from two lessons back.
খাওয়া (khāwā) is Sanskrit √খাদ্ (√khād, "to chew, to bite"), smoothed through Prakrit khā-. Every neighbour eats with it: Hindi khānā, Marathi khāṇe, Gujarati khāvũ, Punjabi khāṇā.

Past Sanskrit the trail goes cold. Khād- has no secure Indo-European pedigree outside Indo-Aryan, so there is no English cousin here — and one will not be manufactured. Some roots are simply local, and saying so is part of the method.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: খ against ক

segments.text: খ is kh: a k with a puff of breath behind it. Its plain partner ক (k) is the letter in Chapter 5's kāj. The puff is not decoration — it is the whole difference between two words, and Bengali gives each its own letter.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: Bengali eats its drinks

utterances: জল খাওয়া (jôl khāwā) means to drink water — "water-eat".
চা খাওয়া (chā khāwā) means to drink tea.
ওষুধ খাওয়া (oshudh khāwā) means to take medicine.

segments.text: Hindi keeps a second verb, pīnā, for drinking. Bengali's everyday speech does not bother: whatever goes in the mouth is khāwā. There is a drink-verb — পান করা (pān kôrā), noun-plus-kôrā in exactly Chapter 5's kāj kôrā shape, built on Sanskrit √পা (√pā, "to drink"), whose Latin cousin pōtāre gives English potion and potable. But it belongs to writing and ceremony. Ask for tea in a Kolkata kitchen and you eat it.

segments.instruction: the drinking Bengali eats — "jôl khāwā … chā khāwā"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the drinking Bengali eats — "jôl khāwā … chā khāwā"]

segments.instruction: the formal drink-verb and its English cousins — "pān kôrā … potion, potable"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the formal drink-verb and its English cousins — "pān kôrā … potion, potable"]

segments.text: How do you say "drink water" in everyday Bengali? (জল খাওয়া — literally "water-eat.") Which Sanskrit root is khāwā, and does English share it? (√khād, "to chew" — and no, the root goes no further than Indo-Aryan.) Which verb would a formal text use for drinking, and what English words does its root reach? (পান করা, from √pā — English potion, potable.) Next: one spelling, two vowels.

lessons.title: দেখা (dækhā) — "to see," and a vowel that moves under a fixed spelling
lessons.gloss: to see, to look — and the vowel that changes while the spelling stands still

segments.text: Chapter 4 buried this verb inside dækhā hôbe, "a seeing will happen." Prised out on its own, it carries a sound rule that runs through every verb in this chapter.
দেখা — dækhā — to see, to look.
আমি দেখি (āmi dekhi), "I see." সে দেখে (se dækhe), "he sees." Read those two romanizations again — they are not the same vowel.

দেখা (dækhā) is traced to Sanskrit √দৃশ্ (√dṛś, "to see") through the Prakrit stem dekkha-; Hindi's dekhnā is the same word. Sanskrit built darśana, "a viewing," on that root, and further back it is PIE derḱ-, "to see clearly." Greek took it for dérkomai, "I look," and for drákōn, the sharp-gazing serpent — which English borrowed as dragon. Bengali's "see" and England's dragons are one word, wearing very different clothes.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: দে, said two ways

segments.text: দ is a soft dental d, tongue on the teeth. The vowel sign ে on it is written identically every time — but Bengali says it either as a close e (as in English bay) or an open æ (as in English bat), and the page will never tell you which.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the ending decides the vowel

utterances: Bengali: আমি দেখি. said: dekhi — close e.
Bengali: সে দেখে. said: dækhe — open æ.
Bengali: তুমি দেখো. said: dækho — open æ.

segments.text: The rule: when the ending carries the high vowel -i, the stem vowel closes to e. Any other ending leaves it open at æ. That is vowel harmony, and the verb of the first lesson does it too — আমি হই (hôi, closed) against সে হয় (hôy, open). It is a rule your ear must carry alone, because the spelling never budges.

segments.instruction: the same shift on the be-verb — "hôi … hôy"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the same shift on the be-verb — "hôi … hôy"]

segments.instruction: the root and its odd English relative — "dṛś … dragon"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the root and its odd English relative — "dṛś … dragon"]

segments.text: Which ending closes the stem vowel to e? (The -i of "I" — dekhi, against dækhe and dækho.) Does the spelling record that? (No — দে is written the same either way; only the ear knows.) Which English animal shares this verb's root? (The dragon — Greek drákōn, from PIE derḱ-.) Next: the last verb, and the knowing English lost.

lessons.title: জানা (jānā) — "to know," and the knowing English gave up
lessons.gloss: to know a fact — beside চেনা, the second knowing that English merged away

segments.text: Six thousand years ago this verb and the English word you are reading it with were the same word. They still are. But Bengali kept a distinction English threw away.
জানা — jānā — to know.
আমি জানি (āmi jāni), "I know." আপনি জানেন (āpni jānen), respectfully.

জানা (jānā) is Sanskrit √জ্ঞা (√jñā, "to know"), the root under jñāna, "knowledge." Behind it stands PIE ǵneh₃-, and English is full of its children: know and knowledge by the direct Germanic road; notice, recognize and cognition through Latin nōscere; gnosis and diagnosis through Greek gignṓskein. Bengali jāni and English know are one verb, separated only by time.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: জ্ঞ, the letter that lies

segments.text: Sanskrit writes the root with জ্ঞ, a knot of j and ñ. Bengali does not say jñ at all — it says gg, so jñāna comes out ggān. The plain verb spares you the knot: জানা (jānā) is simply জা + না, jā-nā.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two knowings, and English has one word for both

utterances: Bengali: জানা (jānā). what it knows: a fact, or how to do something.
Bengali: চেনা (chenā). what it knows: a person or a place, by acquaintance.

segments.text: আমি জানি — "I know" (that it is so). আমি তাকে চিনি (āmi tāke chini) — "I know him," meaning I am acquainted with him. Say jāni of a person and you have said you know facts about them, which is a colder thing.

English once had this line and lost it; French still walks it as savoir against connaître, German as wissen against kennen, Spanish as saber against conocer. And listen to chini beside সে চেনে (se chæne): the same vowel harmony as the last lesson, on a brand-new verb.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: the other knowing — "āmi tāke chini"]

segments.instruction: the six verbs of this chapter — "hôwā, jāwā, āsā, khāwā, dækhā, jānā"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the six verbs of this chapter — "hôwā, jāwā, āsā, khāwā, dækhā, jānā"]

segments.text: Which verb knows a person, and which knows a fact? (চেনা for people, জানা (jānā) for facts — the connaître / savoir line.) Name three English children of this root. (Know, notice, diagnosis — Germanic, Latin, Greek.) Why does chini close its vowel where chæne keeps it open? (Vowel harmony — the -i ending closes the stem vowel, as in dekhi.) That closes the chapter: six verbs, no gender on any of them, and the respect always sitting in the ending.
